[Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) Interview Experience – Round 3 (LLD Round) 🚀

Round 3 at [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) for SDE2(L5) was a Low Level Design (LLD) interview, and it was a deep dive into how you think, not just what you code.

The primary problem discussed was designing Splitwise. The discussion covered:
• Designing core entities (User, Group, Expense, Transaction)
• Maintaining and updating user balance sheets
• Handling different expense types (equal, exact, percentage)
• Validating balances and ensuring correctness of calculations
• Discussing algorithms to keep balances minimal and consistent
• Trade-offs, edge cases, and extensibility of the design

What stood out in this round was the focus on clarity of thought:
• How cleanly you model real-world problems
• How well you justify design decisions
• How you evolve the design step by step instead of jumping to code

The interviewer was less interested in perfect syntax and more interested in:
✔️ Object modeling
✔️ Responsibility separation
✔️ Correctness & scalability
✔️ Communication of ideas

This round reinforced one key lesson for me:

Good LLD is about simplifying complexity while keeping the system flexible for future changes.

Hope this helps anyone preparing for [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) / FAANG LLD rounds.

🚀 Amazon SDE-2 Interview Experience

Interviewed for the Amazon SDE-2 role in April.
After clearing the OA, I was invited for 5 interview rounds (face-face).

Sharing a brief overview to help others preparing 👇
🧪 Round 1 – Data Structures & Algorithms
Design an efficient solution to find the top-K frequent elements from a large dataset.
Approach:
Used HashMap for frequency counting + Min Heap to keep top-K elements.
Time: `O(n log k)`, Space: `O(n)`.

🧪 Round 2 – Problem Solving (Graphs / Trees)
Find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) in a binary tree.
Approach:
Used DFS recursion, returning node when match found and bubbling results upward.
Focused on edge cases (null nodes, same inputs).

🧪 Round 3 – Low Level Design (LLD)
Design a parking lot system.
Approach:
Defined entities (`Vehicle`, `ParkingSlot`, `Ticket`), used OOP principles, enums, and basic extensibility.
Discussed scalability and edge cases.

🧪 Round 4 – High Level Design (HLD)
Design a URL Shortener.
Approach:
Covered APIs, database schema, hashing vs encoding, scalability, collision handling, and caching (Redis).

🧪 Round 5 – Behavioral (Leadership Principles)
Focus Areas:
* Ownership
* Bias for Action
* Handling conflicts
* Failure & learning

**Tip: STAR format is mandatory. Interviewer drilled deep into decisions and trade-offs.

### 📌 Final Verdict

After completing all rounds, the result was shared as “Not Hired”.
No specific feedback or reason was provided, which is standard for Amazon.

Grateful for the learning experience. Back to improving and moving forward 💪

"So I cleared Amazon's SDE interviews. Here's how it went."

A few days ago, I went through Amazon's interview process, and I wanted to share the experience, both the highs and the reality check that followed.

The Assessment Round

First up was the online assessment. Coding challenges, behavioral questions, and culture fit evaluation. This is where most candidates get filtered out, so clearing this felt like a solid first step.

After passing the assessment, I moved to the interview loop, three rounds back to back:

Round 1: LeetCode

Two medium-level problems. I focused on explaining my thought process clearly, why I chose a particular data structure, what the time complexity was, and how I'd optimize if needed. The problems themselves were manageable if you've put in the prep work.

Round 2: Low-Level Design

One design question, but they really dig deep. It's not just about drawing boxes and arrows, they want to know why you're making each choice. How does your system handle failures? Where are the bottlenecks? Be ready to defend your decisions and adapt on the fly.

Round 3: Behavioral

Five to six questions, all centered around Amazon's Leadership Principles. They're looking for specific examples with measurable outcomes. The STAR method helps, but you need real stories with actual numbers and clear impact.

After all that, I got good feedback and made it through the rounds. But I was placed on the offer waitlist, and ultimately, hiring wrapped up for the season before things could move forward.

It was disappointing. You put in all that effort, clear the bar, and still don't get the outcome you wanted. But I also walked away with confirmation that I'm ready for these roles.

If you know of any SWE roles that might be a good fit, I'd love to connect.

Looking ahead, 2026 is going to be my year. I'm continuing to build, continuing to learn, and staying ready for the next opportunity

My Amazon Interview Experience 🚀

Many people have been asking me about my Amazon interview process so here is my experience in a simple way.

The whole process had three rounds and it was completed in around twenty five days.

𝐑𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐧𝐞 👨💻
This round was fully based on data structures and algorithms. I solved two coding questions in forty five minutes.
The first question was a variation of the Rotten Oranges problem based on BFS and DFS.
The second one was a sliding window variation where I had to track the minimum and maximum in a variable size window.
Along with coding there were questions based on Amazon leadership principles.

𝐑𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐰𝐨 🏗️
This was low level design. I was asked to design a music player using object oriented design and classes.
There were detailed follow up questions and again leadership principle questions during the design discussion.

𝐑𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 ⭐
This was the Bar Raiser round and it was fully based on Amazon leadership principles.
There were two questions and both had deep follow up discussions for around fifteen to twenty minutes each.

After these rounds I got my offer and got selected. It was a great learning experience.
For anyone preparing I would say keep your DSA strong learn basic system design and prepare good leadership principle stories.💡

🧩 [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) Interview Experience — Round 4 (High-Level Design)

This round was a deep dive into System Design, where I was asked to design a Collaborative Editing System (like [Google](https://linkedin.com/company/google) Docs).

The discussion revolved around some core, real-world challenges:

🔹 Real-time collaboration
How multiple users can simultaneously edit the same document with minimal latency.

🔹 Conflict resolution & consistency
Handling concurrent edits using approaches like Operational Transformation (OT) and CRDTs, and understanding the trade-offs between them.

🔹 Scalability & architecture
Designing backend components that can handle millions of concurrent users, efficient fan-out of updates, and low-latency sync.

🔹 Data storage, sync & fault tolerance
Ensuring durability, recovery from failures, and seamless user experience even under network issues.

⏱️ The round lasted 1 hour purely on HLD, followed by 20 minutes on [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) Leadership Principles.
The behavioral discussion focused on:
• Ownership
• Handling ambiguity
• Learning from failures
• Making trade-offs with limited information

[Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) interviews truly test both technical depth and behavioral alignment, and this round was no exception.

# Amazon Software Engineer Interview Guide 2026

Amazon's interview process is uniquely defined by their 16 Leadership Principles, a set of values that shapes every hiring decision. Unlike companies where behavioral interviews are secondary to technical assessment, Amazon treats LP alignment as equally important to coding ability. This guide explains how to demonstrate the Leadership Principles while solving technical problems, how to navigate the Bar Raiser process, and what makes Amazon's evaluation criteria different from other big tech companies.

## What Makes Amazon's Interview Different

Amazon's 16 Leadership Principles aren't corporate platitudes, they're the actual framework interviewers use to evaluate candidates. Every interview round, including technical ones, includes behavioral questions designed to assess LP alignment. An engineer who crushes the coding problems but gives weak LP answers will likely be rejected. An engineer with solid (not perfect) technical skills who demonstrates strong ownership, customer obsession, and bias for action may receive an offer.

The Leadership Principles most relevant to engineering roles include Customer Obsession (starting with the customer and working backwards), Ownership (acting on behalf of the entire company), Dive Deep (staying connected to details), and Bias for Action (valuing calculated risk-taking over analysis paralysis). You don't need to memorize all 16, but you should understand them well enough to recognize which principles your stories demonstrate.

Amazon's interview process includes a "Bar Raiser", an interviewer from outside the hiring team whose job is to maintain hiring standards across the company. The Bar Raiser has veto power: if they vote no, you don't get the job, regardless of how other interviews went. They're typically senior engineers or managers who've completed special training. The Bar Raiser interview is often (but not always) the most challenging round.

Unlike Google or Meta, Amazon's process is faster and more transactional. There's no team matching phase, you interview for a specific team and role. The hiring manager is directly involved and invested in the decision. This means less ambiguity about what you're signing up for, but also less flexibility if the team doesn't turn out to be a good fit.

## How Amazon's Interview Process Works

Amazon's interview process typically takes 2-4 weeks from first contact to offer. It's one of the more efficient big tech processes, partly because there's no committee review or team matching phase. The Online Assessment (OA) serves as an initial filter, followed by phone screens and an onsite "loop" of 4-5 interviews.

### Online Assessment 90-120 minutes

Amazon's OA includes two coding problems and a work simulation section that assesses decision-making through scenario-based questions. The coding problems are typically medium difficulty. The work simulation presents workplace scenarios where you choose how to respond, these questions directly assess Leadership Principle alignment. Take the work simulation seriously; it's not just a formality.

### Phone Screen 45-60 minutes

A technical interview with one coding problem plus 2-3 behavioral questions. The interviewer evaluates both your coding ability and LP alignment simultaneously. Don't be surprised when a coding interviewer transitions to "Tell me about a time when..." questions. Both components matter equally for passing this round.

### Onsite Loop 5-6 hours

The loop consists of 4-5 interviews: typically 2 coding/system design rounds, 1 Bar Raiser round, 1 hiring manager round, and sometimes an additional team member round. Each interviewer is assigned specific Leadership Principles to assess. The Bar Raiser evaluates overall caliber and has veto power. All interviewers submit written feedback before the debrief meeting.

### Debrief & Decision 1-2 weeks

All interviewers meet to discuss your candidacy. Each person shares their hire/no-hire recommendation and the specific LP evidence they collected. The Bar Raiser ensures the bar is maintained. Hiring requires consensus, one strong no vote (especially from the Bar Raiser) typically results in rejection. Decisions usually come within a week of the debrief.

### Coding Interviews

Amazon's coding interviews are standard LeetCode-style problems with a twist: every coding round also includes behavioral questions. You might solve an algorithmic problem and then immediately be asked "Tell me about a time you had to dive deep to find the root cause of a problem." The coding portion uses a collaborative editor; you're expected to write working code, not pseudocode.

Frequently tested topics include trees and graphs (traversals, BFS/DFS, shortest paths), arrays and hashing (two-sum variants, sliding windows, frequency counting), object-oriented design (class structure, design patterns), and string processing. Amazon also asks more OOD-style questions than Google or Meta, designing a parking lot system, an elevator system, or a library management system. These questions test your ability to translate requirements into class hierarchies.

### System Design

System design interviews at Amazon often draw from real Amazon products and services. You might design a recommendation system, an inventory management system, or components of AWS. The interviewer wants to see that you can think about scale, reliability, and customer impact. Amazon builds systems that handle millions of transactions per second; your designs should reflect awareness of that scale.

Common themes include e-commerce systems (shopping cart, checkout flow, inventory management), distributed databases (DynamoDB-style key-value stores, partition strategies), delivery and logistics (route optimization, real-time tracking, warehouse management), and cloud services (designing S3-like storage, Lambda-style compute, load balancing). Connect your technical decisions to customer impact whenever possible, that's the Amazon way.

### Sample Questions

LRU Cache implementation Coding

A classic Amazon question testing data structure design. You need to implement get() and put() operations in O(1) time using a hash map plus doubly-linked list. Interviewers will ask about thread safety and how you'd scale this across multiple machines.

Find the k most frequent elements Coding

Tests your knowledge of heaps and hash maps. The optimal solution uses a hash map for counting plus a min-heap of size k. Be ready to discuss trade-offs between heap-based and quickselect approaches.

Design Amazon's product recommendation system System Design

A common Amazon question testing your understanding of personalization at scale. Key topics include collaborative filtering vs. content-based approaches, real-time vs. batch recommendations, and how to handle the cold-start problem for new users.

### What They're Really Evaluating

Amazon's behavioral interviews are comprehensive and structured. Each interviewer is assigned specific Leadership Principles to assess and will ask 2-3 targeted questions. They're trained to use the STAR method for evaluation, so your answers should follow that format. The interviewer will probe for specifics: Who exactly was involved? What was your specific contribution? What were the measurable results?

### How to Prepare

Prepare 6-8 stories that cover the most common LPs: Customer Obsession, Ownership, Deliver Results, Dive Deep, Bias for Action, Earn Trust, and Have Backbone. Each story should have specific metrics, percentages, dollar amounts, time saved, users impacted. Practice the STAR format until it's natural: Situation (brief context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did, not the team), Result (quantified impact). Amazon interviewers will interrupt to dig deeper; this is normal.

### Sample Behavioral Questions

Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager

This assesses Have Backbone and Earn Trust. Amazon wants engineers who will push back on bad ideas, but respectfully. Describe a specific disagreement, how you handled it constructively, and the outcome, whether you won the argument or not.

Describe a time you had to make a decision without all the data

Tests Bias for Action. Amazon values speed over perfection in many situations. Describe how you gathered available information, made a calculated decision, and course-corrected if needed. Quantify the impact of acting quickly vs. waiting.

Deep Dive: I focused heavily on the Rate Limiter and Consistent Hashing videos.

- Why it matters: Amazon’s retail site and AWS services rely heavily on these to prevent “noisy neighbor” problems.
- The Lesson: Seeing how a request flows through a Load Balancer to a Cache and finally to a DB helped me “Dive Deep” during the interview when the Bar Raiser asked about specific failure points.

## 3. The Technical Depth: “Designing Data-Intensive Applications” (DDIA)

If you want to pass a Senior (L6) interview at Amazon, “Grokking” isn’t enough. You need the “Why.”

How to Digest it: This book is the “Bible” of distributed systems. I focused on Chapter 3 (Storage and Retrieval) and Chapter 5 (Replication).

- The Amazon Connection: Amazon pioneered many distributed systems concepts (like the Dynamo paper). Understanding SSTables, LSM-trees, and Eventual Consistency is non-negotiable here.
- Interview Tip: When discussing databases, don’t just say “NoSQL.” Say, “I’d choose a Dynamo-style store with leaderless replication to ensure high write availability, accepting the trade-off of eventual consistency for the shopping cart service.”

## 4. The Practical Edge: DesignGurus

While Educative provides the basics, DesignGurus offers more modern, complex scenarios like “Design a Web Crawler” or “Design Ticketmaster.”

How it helped: Their courses emphasize the API Design phase. Amazon interviewers often ask you to define the specific`POST` and`GET` requests for your system. DesignGurus taught me to define my data models and API endpoints early, which shows "Bias for Action" and technical clarity.

## 5. The Insider Secret: AWS Architecture Center

This is the “cheat code” for Amazon interviews. If you’re interviewing at Amazon, why not use their own architecture patterns?

What to look for: Search for “Serverless Web Application” or “Event-Driven Architecture” on the AWS Architecture Center.

- The Hack: Instead of saying “a message queue,” say “an SQS-style decoupled queue.” Instead of “a key-value store,” talk about the scaling properties of DynamoDB.
- Impact: It shows you are already familiar with the tools Amazon engineers use every day.

## 6. The Peer Pressure: Pramp (Mock Interviews)

System design is a performance. You can be a genius, but if you can’t explain your thoughts while drawing on a laggy virtual whiteboard, you won’t get the offer.

My Strategy: I did 10 mocks on Pramp.

- Learning to Pivot: In one mock, my partner “broke” my database halfway through. I had to learn to stay calm and introduce Read Replicas or Sharding on the fly.
- The “Amazon Voice”: I used mocks to practice “Invent and Simplify” — taking a complex requirement and breaking it down into three simple microservices.

## 7. The Reference: System Design Primer (GitHub)

This is the best “refresher” for the 48 hours before your interview.

How to use it: Don’t try to learn from it; use it to spot-check your gaps.

- I used the Cheat Sheets to memorize latencies (how much slower is a disk seek vs. a main memory read?).
- Having these numbers memorized allows you to do “Back of the envelope” estimations that prove your design is grounded in reality, not just theory.

## The “Amazon” Framework for Your Interview

If you have an interview coming up, follow this 4-step mental checklist:

1. Clarify (Customer Obsession): Define the scale and the “Who.”
2. High-Level Design (Invent and Simplify): Draw the basic flow. Don’t overcomplicate yet.
3. Deep Dive (Dive Deep): Pick one component (like the DB or the Cache) and explain exactly how it handles a million requests per second.
4. Identify Trade-offs (Ownership): Explicitly state what you are sacrificing (e.g., “We are sacrificing consistency for availability here”).

The Amazon interview isn’t just about the right tech — it’s about the right thinking.

## About me

I am a final-year Electronics and Communication Engineering (ECE) student at NIT Surat, with a strong interest in software development, problem-solving, and core programming concepts. This blog captures my complete journey for the Amazon SDE (6 Months) role, which began with Amazon HackOn and eventually led to a technical interview round. At the time of this interview process, I already held a 6-month internship + full-time offer from Cisco. While this provided security, it also slightly affected the intensity of my preparation — something I reflect upon later in this blog.

## Phase 1 — Amazon HackOn

My journey with Amazon began through Amazon HackOn, where we participated as a team of four. We successfully cleared the initial HackOn round and progressed to the idea submission stage. Unfortunately, we could not move forward from that round.

Even though we didn’t clear HackOn completely, our performance turned out to be significant, as it later became the basis for my selection for the next stage in the hiring process.

## Phase 2 — Online Assessment (Based on HackOn Performance)

On September 4, 2025, I received an email from Amazon inviting me to complete an Online Assessment, explicitly mentioning that it was based on my HackOn performance.

The assessment had a total duration of 1 hour and 45 minutes. The first hour was dedicated to two coding questions, followed by 45 minutes for the Amazon Work Style Simulation Assessment.

The coding questions were of LeetCode Medium difficulty, and I was able to solve both of them in approximately 25 minutes. I ensured that my solutions were efficient, handled edge cases correctly, and followed clean coding practices.

The Work Style Simulation assessment focused on evaluating decision-making, ownership, prioritization, and collaboration. This section clearly reflected Amazon’s leadership principles, requiring careful judgment rather than technical knowledge.

## Phase 3 — Interview Shortlisting

On September 19, 2025, I received an email confirming that I had been shortlisted for the interview round. The initially assigned interview date overlapped with my mid-semester examinations, so I requested a reschedule. Amazon handled this professionally, and my interview was rescheduled smoothly.

## Interview Round — Technical Interview (September 29, 2025)

The interview was conducted on the Amazon Chime platform, lasted for 1 hour, and was taken by two interviewers. The focus of the interview was purely technical.

The first coding problem was a stack-based question, conceptually similar to the Next Greater Element to the right problem. I used a monotonic decreasing stack to solve it efficiently, explained the logic step by step, and discussed the time complexity of O(n) and space complexity of O(n). I was able to solve this problem completely and correctly.

In retrospect, I feel that I should have first explained a brute-force approach before transitioning to the optimized solution. Amazon interviewers value seeing how candidates evolve from a basic solution to an optimal one, and this was an important learning for me.

The second question was based on a directed graph, where the task was to determine whether there exists a city from which all other cities can be reached. I explained a BFS-based approach using a visited array and discussed correctness and complexity. Due to time constraints, the interviewer did not ask me to code the solution, but focused on assessing my conceptual understanding.

## Final Result & Honest Reflection

On October 7, 2025, I received a rejection email from Amazon. While the result was disappointing, I view this interview as a learning milestone rather than a setback.

I believe I did not prepare as deeply as I could have for this interview. Having a Cisco internship + full-time offer subconsciously reduced the urgency of preparation. However, this experience clearly highlighted the level of clarity and structure Amazon expects during interviews.

## Key Learnings from My Amazon Interview Experience

This journey taught me the importance of always explaining the brute-force approach before moving to the optimized solution, maintaining structured thinking, and managing time effectively during interviews. It also reinforced that stack and graph problems are commonly asked at Amazon, and that preparation should never be underestimated, regardless of existing offers.

## Closing Thoughts

Interviewing at Amazon helped me understand how Big Tech evaluates candidates beyond just coding ability. Even without converting the interview, the experience strengthened my confidence and highlighted areas where I can improve.

Every interview is a step forward — as long as we learn from it.
